# Abstract

Reconstructing long-run human population across Sub-Saharan Africa, Madagascar, the Western Indian Ocean and the African Atlantic islands requires reconciling twelve millennia of uneven archaeological field surveys, Arab and European mercantile itineraries, colonial fiscal enumerations and contemporary national censuses. Global gridded compilations such as HYDE and KK10 distribute national historical curves across 5-arcminute cells through continental land-suitability heuristics [@KleinGoldewijk2023; @Kaplan2011KK10]. Across a landmass of 24,43M km² (290.451 active 5-arcminute cells) stretching from the Sahara-Sahel transition and the Nubian Nile through tropical rainforests, highland volcanic plateaus and semi-arid southern savannas to oceanic archipelagos, continental averages blur sharp ecological gradients and obscure pre-colonial political cores. NICETHI provides a bottom-up regional reconstruction spanning 55 contemporary jurisdictions from 10000BC to 2025AD, structured across 23 chronological-regional chapters and paired settlement gazetteers.

NICETHI synthesises 24.537 weighted domestic archaeological site-epoch records (11.199 assigned domestic records across 6.970 unique coordinate sites, with 82,94% drawn from regional registers and scholarly monographs and 0% from crowd-sourced platforms) together with 2.732 northern cross-frontier records across 6.431 scale-adaptive domestic HydroBASINS Level 6 catchments and 383 cross-frontier buffer catchments [@LehnerGrill2013HydroBASINS; @BIRD2022P3K14C; @Hinz2023XRONOS]. Pre-industrial spatial distributions combine dual HYDE 3.5 and KK10 biophysical covariates with two-scale non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) residual kriging across ten chronological horizons (unclamped $\tau_1 = 1,41$, calibrated $\tau_1 = 1,35$, $R^2 = 0,9992$) [@PaciorekSchervish2006], harmonised along the northern Sahara-Sahel frontier with HANDBOOK via 2D screened-Laplace multiplicative blending across 77 pre-1975 benchmark rasters. For the statistical era from 1900AD to 2025AD, strictly pycnophylactic sub-administrative disaggregation enforces exact mass conservation across 30.911 unit-year checks covering up to 607 contemporary administrative polygons per benchmark year (704 polygons in 2025AD), with a worst-case relative error of 5,60e-08 [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries]. Urban dynamics are anchored by 20.959 canonical settlements (20.733 city-proper localities and 226 deduplicated agglomerations, including 15.902 pre-1950 settlements drawn from 47.414 chapter-settlement trajectories and 192.623 dated observations reconciled across a three-phase hierarchy) [@OECD2024Africapolis].

Over the Holocene, aggregate population across NICETHI rose from 108k in 10000BC to 2,4M by 1000BC as Sahelian cereal agriculture, Ethiopian highland farming and early Bantu iron-working expanded across savanna and forest margins [@Phillipson2005AfricanArch; @Bostoen2018BantuFirst]. Classical and mediaeval state formation across Nubia, Aksum, the Inland Niger Delta, Hausaland, the Great Lakes, the Swahili littoral and the Zimbabwe plateau lifted numbers to 10,38M at 0AD, 20,71M in 1000AD and 37,99M by 1500AD [@Connah2001AfricanCivilizations; @McIntosh1995JenneJeno]. Following New World crop adoption (maize and cassava) that raised totals to 69,9M in 1700AD, compounding Atlantic, Saharan and Indian Ocean slave-trade extractions, nineteenth-century warfare and early colonial coercive mortality depressed aggregate totals to 61,42M in 1850AD and slowed recovery to 78,2M in 1900AD [@Curtin1969AtlanticCensus; @Lovejoy2012Transformations; @Manning2014AfricanPop; @FrankemaJerven2014AfricanPop]. Post-1950 mortality decline and sustained fertility then drove an unprecedented eightfold expansion from 141,76M in 1950AD to 1,22B in 2025AD, shifting demographic gravity toward fast-growing metropolitan corridors in West, East and Central Africa.

# Background

Quantitative reconstruction of Sub-Saharan African population history occupies a contentious place in world historical demography. Whereas Eurasian syntheses can cross-check centuries of household tax rolls, parish registers and imperial censuses, Sub-Saharan African documentation before the mid-twentieth century is discontinuous across ecological zones and administrative archives [@Caldwell2002HistoricalPopulation; @Caldwell2013AfricanDemographic]. Early world tabulations led by McEvedy and Jones [@McEvedy1978] assumed low pre-colonial carrying capacities and minimal seventeenth- to nineteenth-century demographic disruption, estimating a smooth continental climb from roughly 46M in 1500AD to 110M in 1900AD. Subsequent historical-demographic revisions overturned that consensus. Patrick Manning reconstructed regional cohorts backwards from 1950AD colonial census baselines while incorporating transatlantic, trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean slave exports, raising early modern Sub-Saharan numbers substantially and identifying protracted stagnation or absolute decline across Atlantic-facing belts between 1700AD and 1880AD [@Manning2010AfricanPop; @Manning2014AfricanPop]. Ewout Frankema and Morten Jerven refined the 1850AD to 1960AD trajectory by benchmarking African mortality and growth rates against analogous tropical agrarian economies in Asia and Latin America, demonstrating that colonial enumerations prior to 1945AD systematically undercounted rural populations by 20% to 40% [@FrankemaJerven2014AfricanPop].

Global gridded models translated national population estimates into spatial rasters, most notably through HYDE and KK10 [@KleinGoldewijk2023; @Kaplan2011KK10]. Yet continental allocation rules face four structural difficulties when applied unmodified to Sub-Saharan Africa and the African ocean islands. First, pre-industrial carrying capacity does not decrease monotonically with elevation or distance from the coast. Across Ethiopia, Eritrea, the Western Rift highlands (Rwanda, Burundi and Kivu), the Kenyan Highlands, the Cameroon Grassfields and central Madagascar, tropical highland zones between 1.400 and 2.600 metres elevation escaped severe holoendemic malaria and trypanosomiasis while capturing orographic rainfall on fertile volcanic and lateritic soils [@Fattovich2010Aksum; @Larson2000HistoryMemory]. Conversely, humid lowland rainforest interiors and tsetse-infested miombo belts supported far sparser pastoral and agrarian densities than standard temperature-precipitation suitability curves imply [@Bostoen2018BantuFirst; @Ehret1990PathsThe].

Second, pre-colonial demographic centres diverged sharply from twentieth-century colonial ports and railway junctions. Long before colonial railways anchored Lagos, Dakar, Abidjan, Nairobi, Kinshasa, Luanda, Lusaka and Johannesburg, African urbanisation clustered along the Inland Niger Delta (Jenne-Jeno and Timbuktu), the Nubian Nile (Kerma, Napata, Meroe and Old Dongola), northern Ethiopian plateaus (Yeha, Aksum, Lalibela and Gondar), Hausaland and Borno (Kano, Katsina, Zaria and Ngazargamo), Yorubaland and Benin (Ile-Ife, Old Oyo and Benin City), the Swahili stone towns (Kilwa Kisiwani, Mombasa, Lamu and Mogadishu) and southern Zambezian stone enclosures (Mapungubwe, Great Zimbabwe and Khami) [@McIntosh1995JenneJeno; @Edwards2004NubianPast; @Phillipson2000FoundationsAfrican; @HortonMiddleton2000Swahili; @Pikirayi2001ZimbabweCulture]. Back-projecting contemporary sub-national administrative shares across millennia misallocates pre-industrial rural and urban mass onto twentieth-century mining towns, coastal export ports and planned administrative capitals (Abuja, Dodoma, Lilongwe, Gaborone, Yamoussoukro and Nouakchott) that barely existed before 1900AD [@Hayashi2007LongTerm].

Third, colonial and post-colonial administrative geometries shifted continuously between 1885AD and 2025AD. Imperial partition carved pre-colonial polities into French West Africa (AOF), French Equatorial Africa (AEF), British colonial protectorates, the Belgian Congo, German East Africa, Kamerun, German South-West Africa, Portuguese Angola and Mozambique, Italian Eritrea and Somalia, and the Union of South Africa [@Weidmann2010CShapes; @Kuczynski1948DemographicSurvey1; @Kuczynski1949DemographicSurvey2]. Following First World War League of Nations mandate redistributions and post-1956 decolonisation, national statistical boundaries underwent repeated internal subdivision - from Nigeria's expansion from 3 regions to 36 states plus the Federal Capital Territory, to the Democratic Republic of the Congo's transition from 6 colonial provinces to 26 provinces in 2015AD, Kenya's 2010AD reorganisation into 47 counties, South Africa's 1994AD creation of 9 post-apartheid provinces and sovereign splits separating Eritrea (1993AD) and South Sudan (2011AD) [@NPC2010NigeriaCensus; @KNBS2019KenyaCensus; @StatsSA2023Census2022; @CBS2009SudanCensus]. Disaggregating census schedules onto static 2025AD polygons introduces severe spatial anachronisms across nineteenth- and twentieth-century benchmarks.

Fourth, Sub-Saharan Africa shares a 5.500 km bioclimatic transition with North Africa across the southern Sahara and Nubian Nile. Treating NICETHI in isolation from HANDBOOK would create an artificial border discontinuity across Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Chad and Sudan. Harmonising both archaeological catchment conditioning and pre-1975 gridded population rasters across that northern frontier ensures smooth continental composition from the Mediterranean coast to the Cape of Good Hope.

## Regional Historiography and Evidentiary Foundations

Constructing a continent-wide African demographic archive requires bridging four distinct scholarly traditions. For the Early to Late Holocene and Iron Age, radiocarbon synthesis initiatives - including p3k14c [@BIRD2022P3K14C], XRONOS [@Hinz2023XRONOS] and the ROCEEH Out of Africa Database [@Kandel2023ROAD] - complement regional field registers such as the Online West African Archaeological Register [@Besse2020OSAAR], the Royal Museum for Central Africa's ADRAC and BantuFirst radiocarbon corpora [@Cornelissen2016RMCA; @Bostoen2018BantuFirst], the Ethiopian ARCCH inventory [@ARCCH2020EthiopiaInventory], the National Museums of Kenya register [@NMK2021KenyaSites], South Africa's SAHRIS database [@SAHRIS2024SouthAfrica], Zimbabwe's NMMZ monuments survey [@NMMZ2022ZimbabweSites] and Madagascar's Institut de Civilisations inventories [@ICM2020MadagascarAtlas]. Regional archaeological syntheses track major population inflections: mid-Holocene Saharan aridification and southward pastoral movement [@Maley2015PopulationsAnd]; early Chadian complexity around 500BC [@Toba2026EmergenceSocial]; Nubian and Meroitic iron-working and riverine state formation [@Adams1977Nubia; @Edwards2004NubianPast; @Humphris2018IronSmelting; @GonzalezRuibal2017SudansEastern]; Aksumite highland urbanisation and Red Sea trade at Adulis [@Fattovich2010Aksum; @Zazzaro2013TheAncient; @Phillipson2000FoundationsAfrican]; clustered urbanism in the Inland Niger Delta [@Mcintosh1981TheInland; @McIntosh1995JenneJeno]; Bantu agricultural dispersals across equatorial forests and southern savannas [@Phillipson2005AfricanArch; @Mitchell2002SouthernAfrica; @CoqueryVidrovitch2005BantuCities]; and stone-built urbanism at Great Zimbabwe and along the Swahili coast [@ShadreckChiri1800WhatWas; @WynneJones2018SwahiliWorld; @WynneJones2018TheMultiple].

For the early modern centuries (1500AD to 1890AD), demographic evidence rests on Arabic chronicles, missionary baptismal and tribute rolls, Portuguese fortress records, Dutch Cape tax rolls (*opgaafrollen*) and quantitative slave-trade registers. John Thornton's reconstruction of seventeenth-century Kingdom of Kongo baptismal records demonstrated that pre-colonial Central African kingdoms sustained dense rural populations before civil war and export slaving eroded demographic surpluses [@Thornton1977KongoDemography]. Comparable monographic anchors illuminate Oyo's imperial expansion and frontier domestic economy [@Law1977OyoEmpire; @Ogundiran2009OyoFrontier], Upper Guinea Atlantic ports such as Geba [@Havik2007PortOfGeba], Sahelian governance from Mali and Songhai to Massina, Kong, Samori's state, the Sokoto Caliphate, Kano's plantation estates, Dar Fur and Funj Sinnar [@Davis2000LeadershipStrategies; @Last1967SokotoCaliphate; @Hamza2004DorayiKano; @Azarya1980TradersAnd; @Ofahey1980StateDarFur; @Spaulding1985HeroicAge], Solomonic Ethiopian urban networks [@Pankhurst1982EthiopianTowns], coastal Portuguese fortresses and Zambezi *prazos* in Mozambique [@Pradines2016PortugueseFortresses; @Newitt1995Mozambique; @Gilbert1970CoastalEast], southwestern Cape slavery, settler frontier movement and Khoikhoi demographic contraction between 1652AD and 1780AD [@Shell1994ChildrenBondage; @ElphickGiliomee1989Shaping; @LaCroix2016KhoikhoiPopulation; @Guelke1976FrontierSettlement], and Western Indian Ocean plantation and highland economies across Madagascar, the Comoros and Mauritius [@Beaujard2007EastAfricaMadagascar; @Larson2000HistoryMemory; @Campbell1991ImperialMadagascar; @Allen1999SlavesFreedmen]. Philip Curtin's pioneering Atlantic census and Paul Lovejoy's synthesis of continental slavery quantify the scale and regional selectivity of forced removals across Atlantic, Saharan and Indian Ocean routes [@Curtin1969AtlanticCensus; @Lovejoy2012Transformations].

For the colonial statistical transition (1880AD to 1975AD), NICETHI draws directly on archival statistical yearbooks and demographic surveys rather than secondary interpolations: the *Annuaire Statistique de l'Afrique Occidentale Française* [@AOFAnnuaire1936], the *Annuaire Statistique de l'Afrique Équatoriale Française* [@AEFAnnuaire1950], Cardinall's 1931AD Gold Coast review [@Cardinall1932GoldCoast], Robert Kuczynski's exhaustive two-volume critical audit of British colonial enumerations [@Kuczynski1948DemographicSurvey1; @Kuczynski1949DemographicSurvey2], the 1940AD censuses of Portuguese Angola and Mozambique [@Angola1940Censo; @Mozambique1940Censo], the 1955-1957AD Belgian Congo demographic sample survey [@CongoBelge1958Enquete], the 1955-1956AD First Population Census of Sudan [@Sudan1956Census], the 1948AD British East Africa census and C. J. Martin's methodological review [@EastAfrica1948Census; @Martin1961EastAfrica], and the 1956AD Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland census [@CASO1960FederationCensus], cross-checked against historical monographs on labour migration, colonial urbanism and forced labour [@CordellGregory1987AfricanPop; @Mitchell2007IHS; @Manchuelle1997WillingMigrants; @Keese2016WolofSenegal; @Gouellain1975Douala; @Coates2017PreliminaryConsiderations; @Pankhurst1968EconomicHistory; @Omar2001ScrambleHorn; @Fuller2011ItalyColonial; @Frederiksen2013SeeingThe; @Mudeka2016GenderedExclusion]. Contemporary trajectories from 1960AD to 2025AD integrate official post-colonial census reports from national statistical offices across West, Central, Horn, East, Southern and Insular Africa alongside the OECD/SWAC Africapolis morphological agglomeration database [@OECD2024Africapolis; @Simkins2011SouthAfrica].

# Methodology

## Four-Group Territorial Partitioning and Dual Vector-Raster Masking

NICETHI organises 55 contemporary Sub-Saharan African and island jurisdictions (24.427.754 km²; 290.451 active 5-arcminute cells) into 23 chapters grouped into four historical regimes (Figure \ref{fig:hero-nicethi} and Table \ref{tab:nicethi-itinerary}). Group 1 (Ancient and Mediaeval Polities, 10000BC to 1885AD) opens with a pan-continental prehistoric watershed partition (Chapter 1, 16 ecological macro-zones from Mega-Lake Chad and the Nubian Nile to the Kalahari-Namib and Madagascar), followed by four regional polity modules tracking Nubia and Sudan (Kerma, Kush, Meroe, Makuria, Alodia and Funj), Ethiopia and the Horn (D'mt, Aksum, Zagwe, Solomonic highlands and Ifat-Adal), West Africa and the Sahel (Wagadou, Mali, Songhai, Hausa Bakwai, Ile-Ife, Benin and Kanem-Bornu) and the Bantu Expansion across Equatorial, Great Lakes, Swahili and Southern African corridors.

Group 2 (Early Modern Polities and Trade Networks, 1500AD to 1902AD) partitions the continent into five contemporary political spheres: Atlantic West Africa, Equatoria and Angola (Wolof, Asante, Dahomey, Oyo, Kongo, Loango, Kuba and Luba-Lunda); Early Modern Sahel and Sudan (Timbuktu, Segou, Sokoto, Bornu, Wadai, Darfur and Funj-Mahdiyya); Early Modern East Africa and Mozambique (Buganda, Bunyoro, Rwanda, Burundi, Nyamwezi, Omani Zanzibar and Zambezi *prazos*); Pre-Colonial Southern Africa and the Cape Frontier (VOC and British Cape Colony, Xhosa, Zulu, Sotho-Tswana, Boer republics and Mutapa-Rozvi); and the Western Indian Ocean and Atlantic islands (Merina and coastal Madagascar, Mascarenes, Comoros, Cabo Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, Seychelles and Saint Helena).

Group 3 (Colonial Enumerations and Modern Southern Africa, 1880AD to 2026AD) tracks imperial administrative partitions across West Africa and the Sahel, Equatoria, Belgian Congo and Angola, the Horn and Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, East Africa, and South-Central Africa and Mozambique, alongside the continuous modern census series of Southern Africa (Chapter 16, 1902AD to 2026AD, covering 46 Admin-1 units across South Africa, Namibia, Botswana, Lesotho and eSwatini). Group 4 (Post-Colonial National Censuses and Modern Ocean Islands, 1890AD to 2026AD) comprises seven modern provincial modules covering 538 first-level administrative sub-regions across the African Ocean Islands, the Sahel, coastal West Africa, Equatoria-Congo-Angola, the Horn and Sudan, East Africa, and South-Central Africa and Mozambique.

```{r tab-itinerary, results='asis'}
chs <- root_cache[["chapters"]]
df_it <- do.call(rbind, lapply(chs, function(x) {
  d0 <- as.integer(x[["domain"]][[1]])
  d1 <- as.integer(x[["domain"]][[2]])
  fmt_y <- function(y) if (y < 0) paste0(abs(y), "BC") else paste0(y, "AD")
  data.frame(
    Ch = as.integer(x[["index"]]),
    Chapter = x[["title"]],
    Span = paste0(fmt_y(d0), " to ", fmt_y(d1)),
    Regions = as.integer(x[["subregions"]]),
    Cities = as.integer(x[["settlements"]]),
    Terminal = viscount_fmt_pop(x[["pop_end"]]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))
rownames(df_it) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_it,
  "Canonical 23-chapter NICETHI itinerary showing chronological spans, sub-regions, catalogued settlements and terminal benchmark populations.",
  c("Ch.", "Chapter Title", "Domain", "Regions", "Cities", "Terminal Pop."),
  list(label = "tab:nicethi-itinerary", align = c("r", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r"))
)
```

All 23 chapter masks and 17 historical sub-administrative benchmark geometries (10000BC through 2025AD) were constructed through a two-pass historical GIS protocol drawing on 161 vector files (63.519 features) spanning OpenHistoricalMap, HydroBASINS Level 6 watersheds, Murdock ethnographic regions [@Murdock1959Africa; @LehnerGrill2013HydroBASINS], ETH Zurich CShapes 2.0 [@Weidmann2010CShapes], GADM 4.1, HDX COD-AB and geoBoundaries [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries]. Pass-2 independent visual inspection audited 40 regional and epochal crops (23 chapter masks plus 17 sub-administrative benchmarks from 10000BC to 2025AD), purging all low-vertex straight-line ruler artefacts, anachronistic colonial cuts in pre-1885 layers and detached micro-enclaves while ensuring full island rasterisation across Cabo Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, Comoros, Mayotte, Mauritius, Réunion, Seychelles, Rodrigues, Saint Helena and the Chagos archipelago.

## Multi-Repository Archaeological Ingestion and Dual HYDE 3.5 and KK10 Kriging

Pre-industrial spatial population weights rely on 24.537 weighted domestic site-epoch records (11.199 assigned domestic records across 6.970 unique coordinate sites) plus 2.732 cross-frontier records from HANDBOOK, compiled from nineteen primary scholarly and institutional repositories with 0% crowd-sourced content (Table \ref{tab:arch-jurisdictions}). Primary repositories include the Published Excavations Atlas (3.116 domestic records), p3k14c [@BIRD2022P3K14C] (1.620), XRONOS [@Hinz2023XRONOS] (1.313), BantuFirst and RMCA Tervuren ADRAC [@Cornelissen2016RMCA; @Bostoen2018BantuFirst] (1.557 combined), SARD IntChron Southern Africa (456), KITE East Africa 2025 (261), Pleiades [@Pleiades2024Africa] (150), UNESCO African heritage listings (138), ROCEEH ROAD [@Kandel2023ROAD] (99), Inhambane Mozambique heritage surveys (91), South African Iron Age burial registers (60), Cerasoni West African stone-age and iron-age catalogues (51), Hixon Madagascar chronometric registers (29), Al-Thurayya Early Islamic gazetteer entries (14) and curated NICETHI regional monographs (163), alongside 1.910 deduplicated global radiocarbon baseline entries. Across all four NICETHI archaeological jurisdictions, regional registers and academic monographs contribute 82,94% of assigned records - representing a 4,96x assigned-record enrichment and 3,09x unique-coordinate enrichment over the global radiocarbon baseline (2.256 unique baseline sites). Automated data hygiene excluded 125 null-coordinate records and 339 undated entries while downweighting 2.944 durable stone monuments and 7.762 fuzzed site coordinates so megalithic or funerary biases cannot distort residential density.

```{r tab-arch-jurisdictions, results='asis'}
jur <- root_cache[["jurisdiction_arch_coverage"]]
jur_labels <- c(
  west_africa = "West Africa and Sahel",
  east_horn_africa = "East Africa and Horn",
  central_africa = "Central Africa and Angola",
  southern_africa_madagascar = "Southern Africa and Madagascar"
)
rows_j <- lapply(names(jur_labels), function(k) {
  rec <- jur[[k]]
  data.frame(
    Jurisdiction = jur_labels[[k]],
    Assigned = as.integer(rec[["total_sites"]]),
    Unique = as.integer(rec[["unique_coord_sites"]]),
    Regional = as.integer(rec[["regional_sites"]]),
    GlobalC14 = as.integer(rec[["global_c14_sites"]]),
    RegShare = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * as.numeric(rec[["regional_share"]]), 2), "%"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_j <- do.call(rbind, rows_j)
tot_a <- sum(df_j$Assigned)
tot_u <- sum(df_j$Unique)
tot_r <- sum(df_j$Regional)
tot_g <- sum(df_j$GlobalC14)
df_j <- rbind(df_j, data.frame(
  Jurisdiction = "NICETHI Domestic Total",
  Assigned = tot_a,
  Unique = tot_u,
  Regional = tot_r,
  GlobalC14 = tot_g,
  RegShare = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * tot_r / tot_a, 2), "%"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
))
rownames(df_j) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_j,
  "Archaeological site-record provenance across the four NICETHI jurisdictions (0% crowd-sourced content; 6.431 domestic HydroBASINS catchments at 100% dual HYDE 3.5 and KK10 compliance).",
  c("Jurisdiction", "Assigned", "Unique Coords", "Regional/Mono.", "Global C14", "Regional Share"),
  list(label = "tab:arch-jurisdictions", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
)
```

Site observations are aggregated onto 6.431 scale-adaptive domestic HydroBASINS Level 6 catchments covering 24,43M km² (26,33 catchments per 100k km², maximum domestic area 23.489 km², zero catchments exceeding 25.000 km², median Voronoi radius 31,72 km and 90th percentile 49,29 km) plus 383 cross-frontier conditioning catchments along the HANDBOOK border [@LehnerGrill2013HydroBASINS]. Every domestic catchment meets dual HYDE 3.5 and KK10 biophysical covariate compliance (100% pass rate), combining hydrological proximity, coastal access, arable soil fertility and elevation-climate suitability [@KleinGoldewijk2023; @Kaplan2011KK10]. Freeman-Tukey variance-stabilised catchment intensities are regressed against five biophysical covariates via weighted least squares and interpolated across ten chronological horizons using two-scale non-stationary Paciorek-Schervish Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) residual kriging [@PaciorekSchervish2006]:

$$\gamma(u) = c_0 + (1 - c_0)\left[1 - c_1\left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}\,u}{\tau_1}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}\,u}{\tau_1}\right) - c_2\left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}\,u}{\tau_2}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}\,u}{\tau_2}\right)\right]$$

where $u_{ij}$ is the dimensionless geodesic Voronoi lag, unclamped short-range correlation scale $\tau_1 = 1,41$ (clamped $\tau_1 = 1,35$), long-range scale $\tau_2 = 2,90$, mixture weights $c_1 = 0,80$ and $c_2 = 0,20$, and nugget-to-sill ratio $c_0 = 0,04$ (effective short range 43,63 to 45,76 km; residual $R^2 = 0,9991$ to $0,9992$ across all ten horizons).

Biophysical calibration tailored strictly to NICETHI preserves high-elevation tropical agricultural cores across Ethiopia, Rwanda, Burundi, Kivu, the Kenyan Highlands, the Cameroon Grassfields and central Madagascar without artificial altitude darkening, restricts intense fluvial concentration to perennial rivers (Nubian Nile, Inland Niger Delta, Senegal, Chari-Logone, Congo-Ubangi and Zambezi) rather than intermittent desert wadis, maintains continuous savanna and miombo rural backgrounds, and organically prunes hyper-arid Saharan, Namib and Danakil dust. Along the Mauritania-Mali-Niger-Chad-Sudan northern frontier facing HANDBOOK, all 77 pre-1975 benchmark rasters undergo non-blurring 2D screened-Laplace (Helmholtz) multiplicative harmonisation inside a narrow border ribbon ($\le 18$ pixels, screening length 6,5 pixels):

$$\left(\nabla^2 - \kappa^2\right) u = 0, \qquad p_{\text{new}} = p_{\text{old}}\,\exp(u)$$

with Dirichlet log-ratio targets on the single-pixel interface facing HANDBOOK and $u = 0$ in the NICETHI interior, preserving 100% of interior fluvial and highland relief while eliminating artificial border cliffs.

```{r fig-substrata, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig_02_nicethi_kriged_substrata.png",
  "Kriged 5-arcminute population density rasters across NICETHI at 1000BC, 1000AD, 1500AD and 1900AD showing Sahelian, Nubian, Ethiopian, Great Lakes, Swahili and southern highland population cores.",
  "fig:nicethi-substrata",
  list(max_height = "0.40\\textheight")
)
```

## Pycnophylactic Sub-Administrative Disaggregation and Three-Phase Urban Reconciliation

For the statistical era (1900AD to 2025AD), NICETHI applies strictly mass-conserving pycnophylactic dasymetric disaggregation across time-varying historical and modern sub-administrative polygon regimes derived from colonial yearbooks, legislative boundary lineage records and geoBoundaries [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries; @AOFAnnuaire1936; @AEFAnnuaire1950]:

$$\hat{p}_i(t) = P_k(t) \cdot \frac{w_i(t)}{\sum_{j \in \Omega_k} w_j(t)}, \qquad \sum_{i \in \Omega_k} \hat{p}_i(t) = P_k(t)$$

where $P_k(t)$ is the enumerated or log-linearly bracketed population of administrative unit $k$ at year $t$, $\Omega_k$ is the set of active 5-arcminute land cells within polygon $k$, and $w_i(t)$ is the radial kriged rural suitability weight (blended with satellite urban-rural settlement structure from 1975AD onward). Because legislative reorganisations split colonial provinces into progressively finer modern jurisdictions - rising from 5 historical macro-divisions in 1900AD and 7 mandate blocks in 1920AD-1940AD to 119 units in 1950AD, 194 in 1960AD, 371 in 1980AD, 523 in 2000AD and up to 607 active disaggregated units in single contemporary benchmark years (704 polygon geometries in 2025AD) - matching each year to its period-authentic administrative partition prevents post-independence boundary splits from leaking backward into colonial censuses.

Settlement gazetteers across all 23 chapters were compiled through evidence-only multi-wave ingestion from archaeological excavation reports, pre-colonial chronicles, colonial town rolls, national census locality tables and Africapolis [@OECD2024Africapolis], yielding 13.132 canonical settlements (13.131 populated pan-domain series, 18.145 chapter-settlement trajectories and 66.190 dated population observations). A three-phase metropolitan reconciliation pipeline distinguishes legal city-proper limits (12.905 localities) from morphological metropolitan agglomerations (226 deduplicated pan-domain agglomerations; 263 reconciled metro series across national-historical frames), enforcing explicit foundation dates on colonial mining, railway and planned towns (such as Johannesburg 1886, Nairobi 1899, Bulawayo 1893, Elisabethville/Lubumbashi 1910, Abidjan 1903, Nouakchott 1958, Gaborone 1964 and Abuja 1976) so twentieth-century urban hubs never appear anachronistically in pre-colonial benchmarks.

# Testing and Validation

Every geospatial, statistical and documentary layer of NICETHI passed automated quantitative checks and direct optical inspection prior to publication (Table \ref{tab:validation-audit}). Pass-2 mask auditing inspected all 40 territorial and sub-administrative crops (23 chapter masks and 17 epochal benchmarks spanning 10000BC to 2025AD), confirming 99,99% to 100% active land coverage, zero starved sub-regions across all 23 chapters and zero rectangular cuts. Gazetteer exhaustiveness checks across all 23 modules confirmed zero empty sub-regions (every chapter achieves 100% sub-region settlement coverage, from 8/8 in Nubia and Colonial East Africa to 120/120 in Post-Colonial West Africa), strong log-size dispersion (interquartile range 0,47 to 0,98 dex), high unique-peak ratios (0,69 to 1) and low single-tier concentration (top-1 peak share below 3,2% in every chapter).

```{r tab-subadmin-mass, results='asis'}
rep_yrs <- sub_audit[["representative_years"]]
yrs_keep <- c("1900", "1910", "1920", "1940", "1950", "1960", "1970", "1980", "1990", "2000", "2010", "2020", "2025")
reg_labels <- c(
  R06_COLONIAL_1914 = "Colonial Imperial (1914)",
  R07_MANDATES_1925 = "League Mandates (1925)",
  R07_COLONIAL_1940 = "Interwar Colonial (1940)",
  R08_MOD_1950 = "Late Colonial (1950)",
  R08_MOD_1960 = "Independence (1960)",
  R08_MOD_1970 = "Post-Independence (1970)",
  R08_MOD_1980 = "Federal Reorg. (1980)",
  R08_MOD_1990 = "Late Century (1990)",
  R08_MOD_2000 = "Post-1994 Reform (2000)",
  R08_MOD_2010 = "Pre-South Sudan (2010)",
  R08_MOD_2020 = "Modern Admin-1 (2020)",
  R08_MOD_2023 = "Current Admin-1 (2025)"
)
df_sa <- do.call(rbind, lapply(yrs_keep, function(yk) {
  r <- rep_yrs[[yk]]
  rg <- as.character(r[["geometry_regime"]])
  data.frame(
    Year = paste0(yk, "AD"),
    Regime = if (rg %in% names(reg_labels)) reg_labels[[rg]] else rg,
    Units = as.integer(r[["units_disaggregated"]]),
    TargetPop = viscount_fmt_pop(r[["target_mass"]]),
    MaxErr = gsub("[.]", ",", sprintf("%.2e", as.numeric(r[["max_unit_rel_err"]]))),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))
rownames(df_sa) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_sa,
  "Representative benchmark years of pycnophylactic sub-administrative disaggregation across 30.911 unit-year checks (100% pass below 0,01% relative error; worst-case error 5,60e-08).",
  c("Year", "Boundary Regime", "Units", "Enumerated Mass", "Max Unit Rel. Err."),
  list(label = "tab:subadmin-mass", align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"))
)
```

Geostatistical sharpness and texture diagnostics confirm that two-scale Matérn kriging preserves fine fluvial, coastal and highland relief without isotropic Voronoi blurring or float32 noise. Across the audited kriged and population rasters, minimum high-pass spatial sharpness reaches 0,2261 (visual kriged mean 0,2092; population raster mean 0,2149), minimum directional gradient is 0,152 (kriged mean 0,1585), and maximum directional anisotropy stays bounded at 1,2546. Continuity checks across 1AD record a smooth global ratio of 1,2043, while isolated interior zero pixels remain at 1 to 5 cells (well below the 128-cell noise ceiling) and zero of 614 catalogued settlements below 5k inhabitants were lost during rasterisation across 900AD, 1400AD and 1900AD.

Pycnophylactic mass conservation was evaluated across all 81 disaggregated benchmark years from 1900AD to 2025AD (Table \ref{tab:subadmin-mass}). Across 30.911 unit-year evaluations - scaling from 12,93M disaggregated residents across 5 historical colonial divisions in 1900AD to 1,09B directly disaggregated sub-administrative residents across 553 active units in 2025AD (out of 1,22B domain total) - 100% of units conserved enumerated mass within float32 rounding tolerance, with a global worst-case unit relative error of 5,60e-08.

Cross-frontier Helmholtz harmonisation along the northern Mauritania-Mali-Niger-Chad-Sudan seam with HANDBOOK eliminated pre-existing border steps across all 77 pre-1975 rasters. Before harmonisation, cross-border median density steps ranged from 0,39 dex in 1500AD and 0,45 dex in 1800AD to 0,63 dex in 1000AD and 0,64 dex in 1900AD (95th-percentile steps up to 0,73 dex). After 2D screened-Laplace multiplicative blending over the 18-pixel border ribbon (6,5-pixel screening decay), both median and 95th-percentile border steps dropped to 0,00 dex across all 39 active frontier pixel pairs at every audited probe epoch (2000BC, 0AD, 1000AD, 1500AD, 1800AD and 1900AD), while restoring exact interior sub-administrative mass for all post-1700 disaggregated years.

# Results

## Holocene Foraging, Food Production and Early Iron-Age Expansion (10000BC to 1000AD)

Across the twelve millennia captured in NICETHI, Sub-Saharan Africa and its surrounding ocean islands trace four sharply differentiated demographic phases (Table \ref{tab:macro-basins} and Figure \ref{fig:nicethi-trajectories}). During the Early and Middle Holocene (10000BC to 3000BC), aggregate human numbers climbed nearly tenfold from 108k in 10000BC to 499,1k in 6000BC and 1,03M by 3000BC. During the African Humid Period, lacustrine fishing and pastoral communities flourished across a well-watered Sahara-Sahel belt spanning Mega-Lake Chad, the Niger Bend and the Nubian Nile, before mid-Holocene aridification after 4000BC pushed pastoralists southward into the West African savannas, the Ethiopian foothills and the East African Rift [@Maley2015PopulationsAnd; @Phillipson2005AfricanArch]. Early domestication of pearl millet, sorghum, African rice, teff, enset and yams, paired with cattle and small-stock pastoralism, established distinct agricultural hearths in the Sahel, the northern Horn and the Cameroon-Nigeria borderlands [@Murdock1959Africa; @Fattovich2010Aksum].

```{r tab-macro-basins, results='asis'}
yrs_tab <- c("-10000", "-6000", "-3000", "-1000", "0", "500", "1000", "1400", "1500", "1700", "1800", "1850", "1900", "1950", "1980", "2000", "2025")
reg_keys <- c(
  "West Africa & Sahel",
  "Horn of Africa & Sudan",
  "Central Africa & Angola",
  "East Africa & Great Lakes",
  "Southern Africa",
  "African Ocean Islands"
)
fmt_yr_lbl <- function(ys) {
  yi <- as.integer(ys)
  if (yi < 0) paste0(abs(yi), "BC") else paste0(yi, "AD")
}
df_mb <- do.call(rbind, lapply(yrs_tab, function(yk) {
  vals <- sapply(reg_keys, function(rk) viscount_fmt_pop(macro_ser[["regions"]][[rk]][[yk]]))
  tot_v <- viscount_fmt_pop(macro_ser[["total"]][[yk]])
  data.frame(
    Year = fmt_yr_lbl(yk),
    West = vals[[1]],
    Horn = vals[[2]],
    Central = vals[[3]],
    East = vals[[4]],
    South = vals[[5]],
    Islands = vals[[6]],
    Total = tot_v,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))
rownames(df_mb) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_mb,
  "Secular population trajectories across the six NICETHI macro-basins and domain total from 10000BC to 2025AD.",
  c("Year", "West & Sahel", "Horn & Sudan", "Central", "East & Lakes", "Southern", "Islands", "NICETHI Total"),
  list(label = "tab:macro-basins", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
)
```

Between 2000BC and 1000AD, iron metallurgy and agrarian state formation accelerated continental growth. Total population rose from 1,31M in 2000BC to 2,4M in 1000BC, surged past 10,38M at 0AD, and doubled again to 20,71M by 1000AD. Along the Nubian Nile, the Kerma polity (peaking near 14,7k inhabitants at its urban core around 1650BC) gave way to Kushite Napata and industrial Meroe, where monumental iron smelting supported dense riverine villages along the Shendi Reach before Christian kingdoms (Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia) reorganised settlement from the sixth century [@Adams1977Nubia; @Edwards2004NubianPast; @Humphris2018IronSmelting]. In the northern Horn, D'mt and the Aksumite kingdom linked highland grain terraces around Aksum and Yeha to Red Sea commerce through Adulis, sustaining 3,7M inhabitants across the Horn and Sudan by 0AD [@Fattovich2010Aksum; @Zazzaro2013TheAncient; @Phillipson2000FoundationsAfrican].

Simultaneously, West Africa emerged as the continent's largest demographic engine. Clustered urbanism along the Inland Niger Delta at Jenne-Jeno, early social complexity in the southern Chad Basin, Nok iron-working on the Jos Plateau and rising trans-Saharan exchange under Wagadou (Ancient Ghana) lifted West Africa and the Sahel from 914,7k in 1000BC to 4,01M at 0AD and 9,98M by 1000AD [@Toba2026EmergenceSocial; @Mcintosh1981TheInland; @McIntosh1995JenneJeno]. Further south, Bantu-speaking agriculturalists and iron-workers expanded from the Cameroon Grassfields across equatorial rainforest corridors into the Congo Basin, the Great Lakes and southern savannas, raising Central, East and Southern Africa combined from 614,5k in 1000BC to 6,94M by 1000AD [@Bostoen2018BantuFirst; @Ehret1990PathsThe; @Mitchell2002SouthernAfrica]. On Madagascar and the Comoros, Austronesian maritime settlement merged with East African Bantu communities during the first millennium AD, establishing an Indian Ocean island population of 216,6k by 1000AD [@Beaujard2007EastAfricaMadagascar].

## Mediaeval State Consolidation, Crop Diffusion and the Atlantic Shock (1000AD to 1900AD)

Between 1000AD and 1500AD, regional polities and long-distance trade networks carried NICETHI's aggregate population from 20,71M to 37,99M (Figure \ref{fig:nicethi-substrata} panels B and C). In West Africa and the Sahel, Mali, Songhai, Kanem-Bornu, Hausa city-states, Ile-Ife and Benin sustained 17,49M inhabitants by 1500AD [@Connah2001AfricanCivilizations; @Davis2000LeadershipStrategies]. Across the Horn and Sudan, Zagwe and Solomonic highland expansion alongside the Islamic sultanates of Ifat and Adal and the emerging Funj confederacy in Sinnar brought regional totals to 5,79M [@Pankhurst1982EthiopianTowns; @Spaulding1985HeroicAge; @GonzalezRuibal2017SudansEastern]. In Equatorial and East Africa, interlacustrine kingdoms (Kitara, Buganda, Bunyoro, Rwanda and Burundi), Kongo-Luba-Lunda states, Swahili coral-stone ports (Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi and Sofala) and the Zimbabwe plateau states (Great Zimbabwe and Mutapa, where archaeological demographic reassessment places Great Zimbabwe's urban peak near 18k inhabitants within a broader southern Zambezian population of 230k to 275k by 1600AD) lifted Central, East and Southern Africa to 13,99M by 1500AD [@Thornton1977KongoDemography; @HortonMiddleton2000Swahili; @WynneJones2018SwahiliWorld; @Pikirayi2001ZimbabweCulture; @ShadreckChiri1800WhatWas].

```{r fig-trajectories, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig_03_nicethi_macro_trajectories.png",
  "Holocene and modern population trajectories across NICETHI compared against Manning (2014) and Frankema and Jerven (2014) alongside six-basin growth from 1500AD to 2025AD.",
  "fig:nicethi-trajectories",
  list(max_height = "0.40\\textheight")
)
```

The sixteenth and seventeenth centuries produced a temporary surge in carrying capacity as American cultigens - notably maize, cassava, groundnuts and sweet potatoes - spread inward from Atlantic and Indian Ocean ports into humid forest margins and savanna belts. Aggregate NICETHI numbers climbed briskly from 37,99M in 1500AD to 55,45M in 1600AD and reached a pre-colonial peak of 69,9M in 1700AD. Thereafter, however, demographic expansion stalled and reversed for nearly two centuries (Figure \ref{fig:nicethi-trajectories} panel B). Between 1700AD and 1850AD, NICETHI's aggregate population contracted by 12,1%, falling from 69,9M to 64,06M in 1750AD, 63,18M in 1800AD and a trough of 61,42M in 1850AD, before recovering modestly to 64,31M in 1880AD and 78,2M by 1900AD.

This two-century plateau reflects sharply asymmetric regional shocks. West Africa and the Sahel absorbed the steepest early-modern blow: after peaking at 36,31M in 1700AD, the combined impact of peak transatlantic slave exports across Senegambia, the Gold Coast, the Bight of Benin and the Bight of Biafra, Oyo's nineteenth-century collapse, Sahelian droughts and jihad warfare pushed West African totals down to 22,79M by 1850AD before late-nineteenth-century Sokoto, Kano and coastal export-crop stability lifted numbers back to 33,71M in 1900AD [@Curtin1969AtlanticCensus; @Law1977OyoEmpire; @Ogundiran2009OyoFrontier; @Havik2007PortOfGeba; @Last1967SokotoCaliphate; @Hamza2004DorayiKano; @Azarya1980TradersAnd]. Central Africa and Angola experienced an even longer demographic contraction: Atlantic slaving across Kongo, Loango and Angola reduced totals from 9,53M in 1700AD to 7M in 1850AD, and subsequent Congo Free State rubber coercion, French Equatorial concessionary extraction, forced labour in Portuguese Angola and epidemic sleeping sickness drove Central Africa to a historic nadir of 5,51M in 1920AD [@Thornton1977KongoDemography; @Lovejoy2012Transformations; @Coates2017PreliminaryConsiderations; @AEFAnnuaire1950].

Conversely, regions less directly depleted by eighteenth-century Atlantic departures or buoyed by highland agriculture and new trade corridors grew steadily across the same centuries. East Africa and the Great Lakes climbed from 9,26M in 1700AD to 12,56M in 1880AD before rinderpest, drought and caravan-era raiding caused a brief turn-of-the-century dip to 11,94M by 1920AD [@Gilbert1970CoastalEast; @Newitt1995Mozambique; @Pradines2016PortugueseFortresses]. The Horn and Sudan rose from 8,1M in 1700AD to 11,65M in 1820AD before Mahdist warfare and the 1888-1892AD Great Ethiopian Famine (*Kifu Qen*) held totals flat near 11,49M through 1900AD [@Pankhurst1968EconomicHistory; @Ofahey1980StateDarFur; @Omar2001ScrambleHorn]. Southern Africa experienced severe local contractions - notably the 54% collapse of southwestern Cape Khoikhoi numbers from roughly 50k in 1652AD to 23k in 1780AD following land dispossession and the 1713AD smallpox epidemic, followed by early nineteenth-century *Mfecane* dislocations [@LaCroix2016KhoikhoiPopulation; @ElphickGiliomee1989Shaping; @Shell1994ChildrenBondage; @Guelke1976FrontierSettlement] - yet aggregate Southern African totals climbed from 5,26M in 1700AD to 11,82M by 1900AD as mineral industrialisation accelerated around Kimberley and the Witwatersrand [@Simkins2011SouthAfrica]. Across the Indian Ocean islands, Merina state consolidation in highland Madagascar and plantation indenture in Mauritius and Réunion lifted insular numbers from 1,44M in 1700AD to 2,1M by 1900AD [@Larson2000HistoryMemory; @Campbell1991ImperialMadagascar; @Allen1999SlavesFreedmen].

Comparing NICETHI's aggregate curve against Manning (2014) and Frankema and Jerven (2014) clarifies how spatial bottom-up aggregation reconciles continental historiography (Figure \ref{fig:nicethi-trajectories} panel B). At 1700AD, NICETHI's 69,9M Sub-Saharan total lies below Manning's Sub-Saharan back-projection (roughly 79M to 82M once North Africa is excluded, or 121M in his higher Table 4.1 regional edition) [@Manning2014AfricanPop]. Between 1850AD and 1920AD, NICETHI's directly constrained regional sum (61,42M in 1850AD, 78,2M in 1900AD and 87,43M in 1920AD) sits roughly 20% to 25% below Frankema and Jerven's sideways-projected Sub-Saharan trajectory (85M to 118M), reflecting NICETHI's explicit modelling of Central African, Mahdist-Sudanese, Great Ethiopian Famine and East African rinderpest shocks alongside conservative early colonial district counts [@FrankemaJerven2014AfricanPop; @Kuczynski1948DemographicSurvey1; @Kuczynski1949DemographicSurvey2]. By 1950AD to 1960AD, however, once systematic post-war national censuses replace colonial administrative estimates, NICETHI converges closely onto modern statistical baselines (141,76M in 1950AD and 187,7M in 1960AD; 225,45M by 1970AD).

## Colonial Transitions, Post-1950 Acceleration and Regional Divergence (1900AD to 2025AD)

During the twentieth century, Sub-Saharan Africa transitioned from the slowest-growing major world macro-region to the fastest. Between 1900AD and 1950AD, colonial road and rail networks, famine relief, vaccination campaigns and the gradual abolition of forced portage lifted NICETHI's aggregate population by 81,3%, from 78,2M to 141,76M - an average compound rate of 1,2% per annum, though marked by deep regional disparities between booming Southern Africa (11,82M to 25,47M) and slowly recovering Central Africa (6,89M to 13,19M) [@CordellGregory1987AfricanPop; @Mitchell2007IHS; @Frederiksen2013SeeingThe; @Mudeka2016GenderedExclusion]. Colonial labour corridors - Soninke migration from the Senegal River valley, Wolof groundnut expansion, Gold Coast cocoa booms, Copperbelt mining towns and Southern Rhodesian urban labour circuits - began shifting populations from interior savannas toward coastal ports and mining belts [@Manchuelle1997WillingMigrants; @Keese2016WolofSenegal; @Cardinall1932GoldCoast; @Gouellain1975Douala; @Fuller2011ItalyColonial].

After 1950AD, rapid declines in infant and child mortality paired with persistently high total fertility rates initiated an extraordinary demographic expansion (Figure \ref{fig:nicethi-trajectories} panel C). Total NICETHI population doubled in under three decades from 141,76M in 1950AD to 304,11M in 1980AD, doubled again to 619,9M by 2000AD, crossed 1B shortly before 2020AD (1,04B in 2020AD) and reached 1,22B in 2025AD - an 8,6-fold increase in 75 years (mean annual growth 2,91% per annum) and a mean continental density of 49,96 inhabitants per km² across 24,43M km².

Growth since 1950AD has been shared across every macro-basin, yet asynchronous fertility transitions have steadily reshaped continental shares. West Africa and the Sahel remain the largest demographic bloc, surging more than eightfold from 56,51M in 1950AD to 469,32M in 2025AD (38,45% of NICETHI), propelled by Nigeria, Ghana, Ivory Coast, Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, where fertility decline in the Sahel remains incipient despite rapid rural-urban migration [@NPC2010NigeriaCensus; @GSS2021GhanaPHC; @INS2022CoteIvoireRGPH; @ANSD2024SenegalRGPH5; @INSD2022BurkinaRGPH5; @INSTAT2023MaliRGPH5; @Mbaye2023FertilityEmployment; @Doumbia2019EthnographyUrban; @Souza2014EvidenceFor]. East Africa and the Great Lakes recorded the highest post-1950 multiplier, rising nearly tenfold from 22,74M in 1950AD to 223,2M in 2025AD (18,29% share), reaching 104,81 inhabitants per km² across Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi [@KNBS2019KenyaCensus; @NBSTanzania2022Census; @UBOS2024UgandaCensus; @Golaz2011TheVulnerability; @Kathare2024TheRole].

The Horn of Africa and Sudan expanded nearly tenfold from 20,18M in 1950AD to 195,19M in 2025AD (15,99% share) despite recurring droughts, Eritrea's independence war, South Sudan's secession and protracted regional displacement across Somalia and Sudan [@CSA2010EthiopiaCensus; @CBS2009SudanCensus; @Alemu2026SpatialDistribution; @Bank2015EasternAfrica]. Central Africa and Angola grew tenfold from 13,19M in 1950AD to 132,19M in 2025AD (10,83% share), led by explosive expansion in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola and Cameroon [@INE2016AngolaRGPH; @BUCREP2010CameroonRGPH; @Bank2022AngolaThird; @Bank2021CentralAfrican]. By contrast, Southern Africa - where South Africa, Botswana and Namibia entered sustained fertility decline decades earlier alongside severe 1990s-2000s HIV/AIDS mortality - grew 6,6-fold from 25,47M in 1950AD to 167,51M in 2025AD (13,72% share), while Mozambique, Zambia, Malawi and Zimbabwe maintained brisker expansion [@StatsSA2023Census2022; @Simkins2011SouthAfrica; @StatsBotswana2022Census; @NSA2024NamibiaCensus; @Monamo2026EstimationDistrict; @ZIMSTAT2023ZimbabweCensus; @INEMozambique2019RGPH; @ZamStats2023ZambiaCensus; @NSOMalawi2019Census; @Bank2023SouthernAfrica]. Across the African Ocean Islands, rapid demographic transition in Mauritius, Réunion and Seychelles contrasted sharply with sustained high growth in Madagascar and Comoros, lifting insular totals ninefold from 3,66M in 1950AD to 33,07M in 2025AD [@INSTAT2020MadagascarRGPH3; @INSEE2023ReunionMayotte; @StatsMauritius2023Census2022; @Garchitorena2025ChangesChild].

## Pan-African Urban Hierarchy and Metropolitan Concentration

Tracking 20.959 canonical settlements across ten centuries exposes a structural transformation in African urban rank-size geometry (Figure \ref{fig:nicethi-urban} and Table \ref{tab:urban-hierarchy}). Pre-industrial urban networks across Sub-Saharan Africa were markedly polycentric rather than primate: Zipf rank-size slopes measured across the upper urban tail rose steadily from $q = 0,44$ in 1000AD (when Nubian, Aksumite, Sahelian, forest-belt and Swahili towns formed dispersed regional nodes) to $q = 0,52$ in 1500AD and $q = 0,62$ in 1850AD as hundreds of Yoruba, Hausa, Akan, Sahelian, Kongo, Ethiopian, Great Lakes, Tswana and Merina centres shared demographic weight [@McIntosh1995JenneJeno; @Connah2001AfricanCivilizations; @CoqueryVidrovitch2005BantuCities]. Colonial railway and port concentration steepened the hierarchy to $q = 0,75$ by 1950AD, and post-independence metropolitan primacy pushed the rank-size exponent to $q = 0,92$ by 2020AD. Within individual post-colonial regional chapters, Zipf fits tighten sharply ($R^2 = 0,975$ to $0,996$), reflecting mature national urban hierarchies anchored by dominant commercial capitals.

```{r fig-urban, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig_04_nicethi_urban_hierarchy.png",
  "Rank-size urban evolution across five epochs from 1000AD to 2020AD alongside historical growth trajectories of eight major Sub-Saharan African metropolises from 1800AD to 2025AD.",
  "fig:nicethi-urban",
  list(max_height = "0.40\\textheight")
)
```

Table \ref{tab:urban-hierarchy} lists the twenty leading distinct urban agglomerations and morphological corridors in NICETHI's reconciled pan-African hierarchy [@OECD2024Africapolis]. Lagos (16,11M), Nairobi (15,95M), Kinshasa (11,94M), Johannesburg (11,01M), Luanda (10,2M) and Khartoum (9,62M) have all crossed or approached the 10M megacity threshold, followed closely by Dar es Salaam (6,89M), Abidjan (6,72M), Kano (6,43M), Kampala (6,11M), Yaoundé (5,46M), Accra (5,43M), Addis Ababa (4,89M), Ibadan (4,6M), Dakar (4,39M), Cape Town (4,39M), Bamako (4,24M), Douala (4,11M), Lubumbashi (3,92M) and Abuja (3,86M). Two morphological phenomena stand out in the Africapolis-reconciled urban table and warrant explicit methodological clarity: densely settled agricultural-urban conurbations around Lake Victoria (centred on Kisumu, 17,56M within its continuous peri-urban built-up footprint, alongside Embu at 4,46M and Mbale at 4,15M) and southeastern Nigeria's Igbo-belt corridor (centred on Onitsha, 10,35M) represent continuous rural-urban settlement blankets where morphological built-up thresholds merge dozens of historic market towns and high-density rural parishes into single contiguous clusters, contrasting sharply with compact legal city-proper municipalities such as Dar es Salaam proper (5,38M), Nairobi proper (4,4M) or Maputo and Beira's rapidly densifying informal peripheries [@OECD2024Africapolis; @Mottelson2023UrbanDensity; @Shannon2018SustainableUrbanization].

```{r tab-urban-hierarchy, results='asis'}
tops <- urb_hier[["top_settlements"]]
stem_reg <- c(
  postcolonial_west_africa = "West Africa",
  postcolonial_sahel = "Sahel",
  postcolonial_congo_angola = "Central Africa",
  postcolonial_horn_sudan = "Horn & Sudan",
  postcolonial_east_africa = "East Africa",
  modern_southern_africa = "Southern Africa",
  postcolonial_south_central = "South-Central",
  modern_african_islands = "Ocean Islands"
)
seen_base <- character(0)
rows_u <- list()
for (rec in tops) {
  nm <- as.character(rec[["name"]])
  base_nm <- trimws(gsub("\\s*\\(Agglomeration\\)$", "", nm))
  base_key <- tolower(paste0(base_nm, "-", rec[["country"]]))
  if (grepl("khar", tolower(base_nm)) && any(grepl("khartoum", seen_base))) next
  if (grepl("adis abeba", tolower(base_nm)) && any(grepl("addis ababa", seen_base))) next
  if (base_key %in% seen_base) next
  seen_base <- c(seen_base, base_key)
  sc <- if (identical(rec[["population_scope"]], "metro")) "Agglomeration" else "Morph. corridor"
  if (base_nm %in% c("Kano", "Ibadan")) sc <- "Urban core"
  st <- as.character(rec[["chapter_stem"]])
  rows_u[[length(rows_u) + 1L]] <- data.frame(
    Rank = length(rows_u) + 1L,
    City = base_nm,
    Country = as.character(rec[["country"]]),
    Region = if (st %in% names(stem_reg)) stem_reg[[st]] else st,
    Scope = sc,
    PeakYear = paste0(as.integer(rec[["peak_year"]]), "AD"),
    PeakPop = viscount_fmt_pop(rec[["peak_pop"]]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  if (length(rows_u) >= 20L) break
}
df_u <- do.call(rbind, rows_u)
rownames(df_u) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_u,
  "Leading twenty distinct Sub-Saharan African urban agglomerations and morphological corridors in NICETHI's reconciled pan-domain hierarchy (20.959 canonical settlements; 226 deduplicated agglomerations).",
  c("Rank", "Urban Centre", "Country", "Macro-Region", "Spatial Scope", "Peak Yr.", "Peak Pop."),
  list(label = "tab:urban-hierarchy", align = c("r", "l", "l", "l", "l", "r", "r"))
)
```

# Limitations

Five evidentiary and methodological boundaries qualify NICETHI's reconstructions and define priorities for subsequent revision. First, pre-colonial archaeological survey intensity remains highly uneven across the continent. Well-investigated corridors - the Nubian Nile, the Inland Niger Delta, the Cameroon-Gabon forest fringe, the Rift Valley highlands, the Swahili littoral and South Africa's Highveld and Cape - supply far denser site inventories than the inner Congo rainforest, South Sudan's Sudd marshes, eastern Angola, northern Mozambique or interior Somalia [@Phillipson2005AfricanArch; @Cornelissen2016RMCA; @SAHRIS2024SouthAfrica]. Although Freeman-Tukey variance stabilisation, empirical Bayes shrinkage and dual HYDE 3.5 and KK10 biophysical residual kriging prevent unexcavated basins from collapsing to zero, spatial density contrasts prior to 1500AD remain better constrained in surveyed basins than in low-visibility forest interiors.

Second, early-modern aggregate population levels between 1650AD and 1890AD remain subject to a structural historiographical bandwidth of roughly 15% to 25%. Because virtually no comprehensive household censuses survive outside Dutch Cape *opgaafrollen*, Portuguese island counts and selective missionary registers, reconciling Atlantic and Indian Ocean slave-export mortality with agricultural recovery rates depends on assumed base fertility and indirect warfare-famine multipliers [@Curtin1969AtlanticCensus; @Manning2014AfricanPop; @FrankemaJerven2014AfricanPop]. NICETHI anchors early-modern provincial envelopes conservatively to local historical monographs and regional carrying capacities, positioning its 1850AD-1900AD trajectory below Frankema and Jerven's sideways benchmark while preserving documented regional contractions in West and Central Africa.

Third, colonial enumerations prior to 1948AD systematically undercounted mobile pastoralists, remote forest communities and tax-evading rural households, as Kuczynski documented in exhaustive detail across British West and East Africa [@Kuczynski1948DemographicSurvey1; @Kuczynski1949DemographicSurvey2; @Martin1961EastAfrica]. Even after 1960AD, political contestation and civil conflict disrupted national statistical schedules in several major states: Nigeria has not completed a census since 2006AD (and its 1963AD census suffered documented regional inflation) [@NPC2010NigeriaCensus; @FrankemaJerven2014AfricanPop]; the Democratic Republic of the Congo's last full enumeration occurred in 1984AD; Somalia last conducted a partial count in 1975AD; Eritrea has held no post-independence census; and Ethiopia's last published national census dates to 2007AD [@CSA2010EthiopiaCensus]. For those jurisdictions, post-2010 sub-administrative targets necessarily combine official national projections with satellite-assisted settlement distributions.

Fourth, morphological urban definitions diverge sharply from legal municipal jurisdictions across densely settled agrarian regions. In the Lake Victoria basin (Kisumu, Mbale), the Kenyan Highlands (Nairobi-Embu), Burundi-Rwanda (Kayanza) and southeastern Nigeria (Onitsha-Awka-Nnewi), Africapolis built-up contiguity rules merge dense smallholder settlement belts into multi-million morphological clusters whose populations exceed legal municipal boundaries by a factor of three to ten [@OECD2024Africapolis]. NICETHI explicitly flags spatial scope (city-proper versus agglomeration or morphological corridor) so analysts can select consistent urban thresholds rather than conflating municipal cores with peri-urban belts.

Fifth, mobile pastoralists across the Sahel, Horn, Rift Valley and Kalahari-Namib leave ephemeral residential footprints and cross international boundaries seasonally, causing modest inter-annual reallocation uncertainty along arid frontier polygons in Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Chad, Sudan, Somalia, Kenya and Namibia.

# Conclusion

NICETHI delivers a unified, spatially explicit twelve-millennium demographic reconstruction covering 24,43M km² and 55 contemporary jurisdictions across Sub-Saharan Africa, Madagascar, the Western Indian Ocean and the African Atlantic islands. Integrating 24.537 weighted domestic archaeological site-epoch observations (82,94% regional and scholarly provenance, 0% crowd-sourced), 6.431 scale-adaptive HydroBASINS catchments meeting 100% dual HYDE 3.5 and KK10 biophysical compliance, two-scale non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) residual kriging across ten horizons ($R^2 = 0,9992$), 2D screened-Laplace northern frontier harmonisation with HANDBOOK across 77 pre-1975 benchmark rasters, strictly pycnophylactic sub-administrative disaggregation across 30.911 unit-year checks (maximum relative error 5,60e-08) and 13.132 canonical settlements (263 reconciled metropolitan series), NICETHI bridges prehistoric regional archaeology and twenty-first-century sub-national demography within a single internally consistent spatial archive.

Viewing Sub-Saharan Africa and its adjacent oceanic islands across twelve millennia clarifies three enduring demographic patterns. First, ecological heterogeneity - above all the interplay of highland volcanic refugia, perennial floodplains, savanna-forest ecotones and tropical disease vectors - shaped pre-industrial population geography far more powerfully than proximity to ocean coasts, anchoring historical cores along the Nubian Nile, the Ethiopian and Great Lakes highlands, the Sahel-savanna belt and southern Zambezian plateaus. Second, the two-century stagnation between 1700AD and 1900AD demonstrates how external slave-trade extraction, coercive colonial labour regimes and nineteenth-century epizootics (rinderpest) temporarily cancelled earlier agricultural carrying-capacity gains from New World crops across West and Central Africa. Third, the post-1950 demographic explosion - lifting numbers more than eightfold from 141,76M to 1,22B in three generations while transforming a historically polycentric settlement network into an archipelago of multi-million metropolitan corridors - represents the most rapid continental redistribution of human population in recorded history. Continuously joined to HANDBOOK across the Sahara-Sahel interface, NICETHI completes the African continental mosaic of Operation Viscount.

# Appendix

## Ten Chronological Kriging Horizons and Variogram Diagnostics

Table \ref{tab:arch-horizons} reports domestic archaeological site totals, active HydroBASINS Level 6 catchments (out of 6.431 domestic basins), unclamped Matérn short-range correlation scales ($\tau_1$), effective short-range distances and residual $R^2$ values across all ten kriging horizons. Weighted archaeological observations peak during the Classical Aksum, Meroe and Jenne-Jeno horizon (3.497 site records across 1.323 active basins) before tapering naturally in the nineteenth-century pre-colonial horizon (1.130 archaeological records across 547 basins), where written itineraries, missionary counts and early colonial registers supersede excavated sites as primary spatial anchors. Across all ten horizons, non-stationary Matérn variogram fits maintain residual $R^2$ between 0,9991 and 0,9992 with remarkably stable unclamped $\tau_1$ values (1,38 to 1,44, effective short range 43,63 to 45,76 km).

```{r tab-arch-horizons, results='asis'}
p_gjs <- root_cache[["period_geojsons"]]
vmods <- krig_diag[["variogram_models"]]
h_labels <- c(
  "01_late_pleistocene_early_holocene" = "Late Pleistocene & Early Holocene (10000BC-6000BC)",
  "02_mid_holocene_pastoral_neolithic" = "Mid-Holocene Pastoral Neolithic (6000BC-3000BC)",
  "03_kerma_late_neolithic_pre_iron" = "Kerma & Late Neolithic Pre-Iron (3000BC-1000BC)",
  "04_early_iron_age_kush_nok_bantu" = "Early Iron Age: Kush, Nok & Bantu (1000BC-300BC)",
  "05_classical_axum_meroe_jenneno" = "Classical Aksum, Meroe & Jenne-Jeno (300BC-400AD)",
  "06_late_antique_nubia_ghana_swahili" = "Late Antique Nubia, Ghana & Swahili (400AD-800AD)",
  "07_early_mediaeval_sahel_great_lakes" = "Early Mediaeval Sahel & Great Lakes (800AD-1200AD)",
  "08_high_mediaeval_mali_zimbabwe_solomonic" = "High Mediaeval Mali, Zimbabwe & Solomonic (1200AD-1500AD)",
  "09_early_modern_atlantic_sahel_swahili" = "Early Modern Atlantic, Sahel & Swahili (1500AD-1800AD)",
  "10_late_precolonial_nineteenth_century" = "Late Pre-Colonial Nineteenth Century (1800AD-1900AD)"
)
df_ah <- do.call(rbind, lapply(p_gjs, function(p) {
  k <- p[["key"]]
  vm <- vmods[[k]]
  data.frame(
    Horizon = if (k %in% names(h_labels)) h_labels[[k]] else k,
    Sites = as.integer(p[["total_sites_count"]]),
    Basins = as.integer(p[["active_domestic_catchments"]]),
    RawTau1 = viscount_fmt_number(vm[["raw_tau1_dimensionless"]], 2),
    RangeKm = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(vm[["effective_short_range_km"]], 1), " km"),
    R2 = viscount_fmt_number(vm[["residual_r2"]], 4),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))
rownames(df_ah) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_ah,
  "Weighted domestic archaeological site observations, active HydroBASINS Level 6 catchments (out of 6.431) and Matérn variogram parameters across ten chronological horizons.",
  c("Chronological Horizon", "Sites", "Basins", "Raw Tau-1", "Short Range", "Residual R²"),
  list(label = "tab:arch-horizons", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
)
```

## Historiographic Benchmark Comparison (1700AD to 1960AD)

To situate NICETHI transparently against established continental demographic series [@McEvedy1978; @Manning2010AfricanPop; @Manning2014AfricanPop; @FrankemaJerven2014AfricanPop], Table \ref{tab:historiographic-comp} juxtaposes NICETHI's Sub-Saharan aggregate against Manning's Table 4.1 Sub-Saharan totals (computed as continental total minus Northern Africa) and Frankema and Jerven's all-Africa census-adjusted projections (1850AD to 1960AD) compiled inside NICETHI's reference benchmark archive. The table highlights both the shared structural finding of pre-1900 stagnation and the narrower gap separating NICETHI from mid-century census totals once decolonisation statistical surveys take hold between 1950AD and 1960AD.

```{r tab-historiographic-comp, results='asis'}
arf_tabs <- root_cache[["arf_regional_population_tables"]]
m_rows <- arf_tabs[[1]][["rows"]]
fj_rows <- arf_tabs[[4]][["rows"]]
m_ssa <- setNames(sapply(m_rows, function(r) as.numeric(r[["Total"]]) - as.numeric(r[["Northern"]])), sapply(m_rows, function(r) as.character(r[["year"]])))
fj_all <- setNames(sapply(fj_rows, function(r) as.numeric(r[["fj_m"]])), sapply(fj_rows, function(r) as.character(r[["year"]])))
m_all_fj <- setNames(sapply(fj_rows, function(r) as.numeric(r[["manning_m"]])), sapply(fj_rows, function(r) as.character(r[["year"]])))

comp_yrs <- c("1700", "1800", "1850", "1880", "1900", "1920", "1940", "1950", "1960")
df_hc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(comp_yrs, function(yk) {
  ni_m <- as.numeric(macro_ser[["total"]][[yk]]) / 1e6
  m_sub_val <- if (yk == "1700") paste0(viscount_fmt_number(m_ssa[["1700"]], 1), "M")
    else if (yk == "1800") paste0(viscount_fmt_number(m_ssa[["1790"]], 1), "M (1790AD)")
    else if (yk == "1880") paste0(viscount_fmt_number(m_ssa[["1890"]], 1), "M (1890AD)")
    else if (yk == "1950") paste0(viscount_fmt_number(m_ssa[["1950"]], 1), "M")
    else "-"
  m_pan_val <- if (yk %in% names(m_all_fj)) paste0(viscount_fmt_number(m_all_fj[[yk]], 1), "M") else "-"
  fj_pan_val <- if (yk %in% names(fj_all)) paste0(viscount_fmt_number(fj_all[[yk]], 1), "M") else "-"
  data.frame(
    Year = paste0(yk, "AD"),
    NICETHI = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(ni_m, 2), "M"),
    ManningSSA = m_sub_val,
    ManningAll = m_pan_val,
    FJAll = fj_pan_val,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))
rownames(df_hc) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_hc,
  "Comparison of NICETHI Sub-Saharan population totals (1700AD to 1960AD) against Manning Table 4.1 Sub-Saharan totals and all-Africa series from Manning (2010) and Frankema and Jerven (2014).",
  c("Year", "NICETHI (SSA)", "Manning (SSA)", "Manning (All Afr.)", "Frankema-Jerven (All)"),
  list(label = "tab:historiographic-comp", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
)
```

## Summary of Geostatistical, Frontier and Sub-Administrative Calibration Parameters

NICETHI's continuous 5-arcminute population surfaces cover 290.451 active land cells across 24,43M km² from 10000BC to 2025AD. Non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) residual kriging across 6.431 domestic HydroBASINS Level 6 catchments (median Voronoi radius 31,72 km; 100% dual HYDE 3.5 and KK10 compliance) and 383 northern frontier catchments yielded an unclamped global short-range scale $\tau_1 = 1,41$ (calibrated $\tau_1 = 1,35$, long-range $\tau_2 = 2,90$, nugget-to-sill ratio 0,04, residual $R^2 = 0,9991$ to $0,9992$). Screened-Laplace multiplicative blending over an 18-pixel border ribbon (screening decay 6,5 pixels) eliminated all pre-existing 0,39 to 0,64 dex border steps against HANDBOOK across 77 pre-1975 rasters (0,00 dex post-harmonisation step across all 39 seam pairs). Pycnophylactic sub-administrative disaggregation enforced exact mass conservation across 81 benchmark years from 1900AD to 2025AD (30.911 unit-year checks, up to 607 active units in a single benchmark year, 100% pass rate, worst-case unit relative error 5,60e-08). Together, these parameters anchor all 23 constituent regional studies and gazetteers into a continuous Sub-Saharan and oceanic population grid.
